Multi-objective optimization seeks designs that balance several conflicting objectives, such as performance and cost, at once. Instead of a single optimum it returns a Pareto front of non-dominated solutions, where improving one objective requires sacrificing another, and evolutionary methods such as the NSGA-II genetic algorithm are commonly used to find it for expensive black-box models.

## Pareto fronts for amine CO2 capture processes (2013)

Lee and co-workers ran NSGA-II over ten design and operating variables of an Aspen Plus capture and compression model, maximizing net plant power and minimizing capital cost for each of three amine solvents ([Lee et al. 2013](/papers/lee2013/)). The fronts exposed a minimum capital cost for 90% capture, a ceiling on net power and diminishing returns in efficiency for added capital, and comparing fronts across solvents gave a fairer ranking than evaluating all solvents in one fixed design. Summary: [lee2013](/papers/lee2013/).
